reviewEvidence.visualReviewMethod: Full-duration six-second contact sampling, reading the English burned-in captions and the posed examples; real-time whole-audio listening not claimed.
reviewEvidence.resolutionNote: Research-only reference media; never a production source. Independent production footage still requires genuine FHD or higher.

centralQuestion: Why do deliberately exaggerated or distorted poses often make an attack read better in a game?
thesis: Judge the motion at the size and speed the player sees it; exaggerated poses and overshoot can preserve energy that small presentation and conservative rigging would otherwise lose.

claims: Kazuya's striking waist twist is an intentional animation choice, not necessarily an accidental defect.
A visually convincing moving result can use deformation that looks extreme in a frozen frame.
sections.observedVisuals: Smash Kazuya Spinning Demon to Left Hook-style rotational kick/waist twist is compared with Tekken 7; arrows identify the waist. Exact displayed move nomenclature still requires canonical verification before production.
sections.exampleRoles: One conspicuous distortion establishes the tension between anatomical correctness and motion readability.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Independent actual gameplay for the observed twist, then our same grid character rotating conservatively versus expressively; no copied lesson clip.
sections.transitionToNext: The extreme close-up must be judged in the actual small gameplay view.

claims: In small on-screen attacks, insufficient motion amplitude is often the bigger problem.
Push an acceptable-looking attack further so its intention and force remain visible.
sections.observedVisuals: Small versus large uppercut-like motion, followed by paired not-enough/just-right views. The source explicitly says it uses different moves to illustrate the difference.
sections.exampleRoles: Amplitude comparison makes the principle visible; it is not a controlled same-move experiment in the source.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Use one shared clip and mannequin with only the intended amplitude changed, then display both at gameplay scale. Label it our controlled illustration.
prerequisites: Define silhouette and motion amplitude through the visible displacement, not just terminology.
sections.transitionToNext: Exaggeration also depends on what the character's rig can actually change.

claims: An older torso-to-arm rig allowed arm-angle changes but not shoulder-position changes.
Human shoulders can move forward and backward, so a rig's permitted transforms affect expressive range.
Improved techniques and tools can support more flexible movement.
sections.observedVisuals: Early Smash/Dragon King prototype followed by the presenter moving shoulders.
sections.exampleRoles: Historical example shows how a restricted representation limits animation, not a mandate to discuss prototype biography.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Our grid rig: fixed shoulder attachment with arm rotation, then permit shoulder translation; annotate the one additional degree of freedom.
prerequisites: Explain joint pivot, rotation and translation through one shoulder before using rig terminology.
sections.transitionToNext: A flexible rig may create odd frozen shapes; repairing every one can remove the intended energy.

claims: Correcting every paused distortion can weaken the moving animation.
Virtua Fighter already used pronounced upper/lower body opposition; physically conservative range is not the only criterion for a useful game pose.
The guiding conclusion is to allow sufficient exaggeration for the moving result.
sections.observedVisuals: Virtua Fighter Lau versus Jacky with enlarged torso/leg opposition and normal gameplay.
sections.exampleRoles: A separate established game confirms that forceful readable motion is not dependent on realistic joint angles.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Independent footage comparison plus a split grid freeze/frame versus normal-speed sequence of our rig; explain why the frame exists in the movement.
sections.transitionToNext: The same idea applies to straight-line changes, through overshoot and return.

claims: A linear movement can go past its settled extent and then retract slightly.
Kirby's Adventure Needle animation illustrates an expanded frame followed by a smaller settled frame.
sections.observedVisuals: Numbered Needle sprite images show frame three overshooting and frame four retracting; normal game view confirms the feel.
sections.exampleRoles: Cross-dimensional extension from 3D poses to a simple 2D overshoot.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Own licensed pixel character or clearly illustrative spike shape on the grid: grow beyond a marked final extent, return, then replay at native speed; separate independent Kirby footage if used.
prerequisites: Define overshoot as passing the final target then returning. Number labels must describe our sample or verified sprite sequence, not invented game measurements.
sections.transitionToNext: Close on the same principle: enough visible movement matters more than conservative isolated frames.

Do not turn the source's strong artistic preference into permission to leave accidental mesh errors unexamined; judge the intended moving result without adding an unrelated defensive disclaimer.
